svg.aria-label: Diagram: the path a resource request takes through Azure Policy, showing the definition supplying the rule and the effect while the assignment supplies scope, notScopes, resource selectors, overrides, enforcement mode and identity, then the fixed order in which effects evaluate with disabled first, append and modify next, then deny, audit, manual and auditIfNotExists, with denyAction last before the Resource Provider, and auditIfNotExists and deployIfNotExists running again only after the Resource Provider returns success
svg.title: Where an Azure Policy rule is decided: the definition states it, the assignment governs it, the effect order settles which one the caller sees
svg.text: The definition is the specification. The assignment is the control.
Six properties on the assignment can each neutralise a correct rule, and none of them appear in the definition anybody reviews.
Policy definition — states the rule, governs nothing
JSON. Reviewable in a pull request. Inert until an assignment picks it up.
policyRule · if / then · exactly one effect
parameters · max 20 · nested conditionals · max 512
mode — all, or indexed
indexed skips every type that cannot carry a tag or a location.
definition location — management group or subscription
Caps for ever where the policy can be assigned. Permanent in practice.
Policy assignment — decides how much of it is real
Often created once in the portal, then never read again.
scope — includes every child container and resource
notScopes — max 400 · excluded from the compliance count
resourceSelectors — max 10 · each list max 50 values
overrides — max 10 × 50 refs · replaces the effect outright
enforcementMode — Default, DoNotEnforce or Enroll
identity — exactly one, and required by modify and DINE
Any one of these can silence the rule without editing it.
Order of evaluation — fixed, and mostly before the Resource Provider ever sees the request
disabled
evaluate at all?
append / modify
alters the request
deny
before audit
audit
records only
manual
attested by a human
auditIfNotExists
looks at a related object
denyAction
evaluated last
append and modify run before deny, so a request they correct is never seen as non-compliant by the deny that would have blocked it.
Resource Provider processes the request
on a success code only
Second pass — auditIfNotExists and deployIfNotExists evaluate again
This is the whole reason deployIfNotExists can only react to a resource that already exists. It never blocks anything; it deploys afterwards,
using the assignment's managed identity — while the existence check that decided whether to run used the requestor's identity instead.
Timing, and the numbers behind most “the policy did not work” reports
A new or updated assignment takes about five minutes to apply to its scope before the evaluation cycle begins for applicable resources.
A resource deployed or updated in scope reports its effect event and compliance status about 15 minutes later, and evaluates nothing else.
Every assignment is reevaluated once every 24 hours on the standard compliance cycle; an on-demand scan is available but is slow.
Layering is cumulative most restrictive, and each assignment is evaluated independently.
There is no merge step and no precedence between assignments. Two reasonable deny rules at two scopes can block a resource neither intended
to block on its own, and the documented remedy is to review the exclusions on each assignment rather than to soften either rule.
Sources: Azure Policy effect basics, definition structure basics, assignment structure, scope, and get compliance data on Microsoft Learn.
